title: Subvert Trust Controls: Mark-of-the-Web Bypass
summary: Windows marks files that arrive from the internet with a hidden stream named Zone.Identifier, and that mark, the Mark-of-the-Web, drives several protective behaviours: Office documents open in Protected View, script hosts refuse or warn, and executables are checked against SmartScreen reputation before running. This sub-technique defeats the mark by delivery rather than by editing it. Archive and disk image formats such as ISO, VHD, ARJ and GZIP are downloaded legitimately, so the container itself is marked, but the files inside are extracted or mounted onto the local disk where the alternate stream is not carried over. The extracted payload is then treated as a local file and runs without Protected View or reputation checks. Defenders can spot the pattern in process lineage: a mount or extraction step immediately preceding execution of a newly written binary from a removable or mounted volume.

beginner.definition: When you download a file, Windows adds a hidden note saying it came from the internet. That note makes Office open documents in a safe view and makes Windows warn before running programs. This sub-technique hides the note by packaging the file inside an archive or disk image first.
beginner.whyItMatters: That hidden note is one of the simplest protections against email and web attacks. When it is missing, files open normally and users see no warning at all. Attackers can therefore send one download that unpacks into many unprotected files. Without monitoring the unpack step, the defence simply never triggers.
howItWorks: Windows tags each downloaded file with a hidden note attached to the file itself.
Software such as Office and Defender reads that note, then adds warnings or safe views.
The attacker puts the harmful file inside an archive or a disk image file.
You download the container, which carries the note, then open it on your machine.
The files inside are written to your local disk and lose that note completely.
Those inner files now run as ordinary local software with no warning.
beginner.example: Think of a parcel arriving from abroad with a customs sticker on the outside box. Inspectors check the sticker and the outer box carefully. Someone then takes the parcel to a back room, opens it, and hands the contents to a colleague. The inner items never carry a sticker, so nobody checks them again. Mounting a disk image is that back room.
takeaways: Container formats such as ISO and VHD can strip protection from the files inside.
Watch for mounting or extraction activity followed by execution from the new volume.
Block or inspect disk image files at the email gateway and on user endpoints.

objectives: Explain what the Mark-of-the-Web is and which protections depend on it.
Describe how archive and disk image containers prevent inner files from inheriting the mark.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from other ways of tampering with trust controls.
Identify the process behaviours that indicate mount or extract followed by execution.
Recommend gateway and endpoint controls that reduce the risk from container files.
